name: Lebanon
headline: A country defaults; a society still holds.
summary: Lebanon long served as the Middle East's financial hub and trading crossroads. Its confessional model maintained a fragile peace, but it also blocked economic decisions. Since 2019 the currency, the banks, and public debt have collapsed; the absence of market prices has itself become a risk signal.

history.title: Greater Lebanon
history.text: France creates Greater Lebanon under mandate. The country brings together Christian and Muslim communities with fragile demographic balances.

history.title: Independence and the National Pact
history.text: An unwritten compromise splits power between Christians and Muslims. The presidency goes to a Maronite, the government to a Sunni, Parliament to a Shia.

history.title: The civil war
history.text: The conflict pits militias and communities against each other, with Syrian and Israeli interventions. Beirut, once a financial center, is destroyed.

history.title: The Taif Accords
history.text: Saudi Arabia sponsors a compromise that ends the war. Power is rebalanced toward Muslims, but confessional rule remains central.

history.title: The Cedar Revolution
history.text: After Rafic Hariri's assassination, mass demonstrations push the Syrian army out. The political class is largely unchanged.

history.title: Collapse and explosion
history.text: The dollar shortage and the eurobond default wipe out most of the currency's value. In August 2020, the Beirut port explosion ravages the capital.

history.title: War and ceasefire
history.text: The conflict between Israel and Hezbollah displaces hundreds of thousands. A ceasefire opens a political window, but economic reforms remain blocked.

institutions.executive: Maronite president, Sunni Prime Minister, and a national-unity government
institutions.legislature: Parliament with confessional allocation, frequently deadlocked
institutions.central_bank: Banque du Liban (BDL), at the heart of the monetary crisis
institutions.currency: Lebanese pound (LBP), an official rate and a parallel market
institutions.law: Civil law based on French law; confessional courts for personal status
institutions.fact: Lebanon has no active sovereign rating and no liquid CDS: the absence of price is treated as a risk, not as neutrality.

allies.name: France
allies.note: Diplomatic and historic support, aid conferences.

allies.name: Saudi Arabia
allies.note: A traditional financial partner, with irregular relations.

allies.name: The diaspora
allies.note: Remittances and networks abroad cushion the crisis.

rivals.name: Israel
rivals.note: Recurrent armed conflict and border tensions.

rivals.name: Hezbollah
rivals.note: An armed and political actor that challenges the state's monopoly.

dependencies.name: Iran
dependencies.note: Support for Hezbollah and political influence.

dependencies.name: Imports
dependencies.note: Food, fuel, and medicine depend on foreign currency.

gdp_growth.note: The economy is still contracting on war and destruction. Recovery will depend on reconstruction and political stability.

inflation.note: Inflation remains extremely high after the pound's collapse. It destroys purchasing power and makes planning impossible.

debt_gdp.note: The debt is in default and largely illiquid. The ratio is an estimate, because public accounting and exchange distortions blur the measure.

policy_rate.note: The official rate no longer reflects market conditions. The banking system is being restructured and capital is frozen.

unemployment.note: Unemployment and the emigration of youth strip the country of its middle class and skills.

reserves.note: Net reserves are low and largely constrained. They cannot restore confidence in the currency.

rating.note: The country is in sovereign default. A D rating means the debt is not being honored on its terms.

cds.note: No liquid CDS: the debt is already in default. Missing data is treated as a maximum-risk signal.

equity_index.note: The market is very illiquid. Prices do not properly reflect asset values in a fragmented, dollarized economy.

currency.name: Lebanese pound
currency.note: The pound has lost most of its value since 2019. The official and parallel rates diverged for a long time.

strengths: An entrepreneurial diaspora and a dense international network.
A historically high level of education.
risks: Sovereign default and an insolvent banking system.
A destroyed currency and a largely dollarized economy.
Political deadlock and the risk of armed conflict.
opportunities: Reconstruction and reform of the electricity sector.
Restoring confidence in banks and deposits.
The return of diaspora capital if an IMF deal is reached.

quiz.question: Which institutional feature makes Lebanese decision-making so hard?
quiz.explanation: The confessional system allocates posts between communities. It preserved a political balance, but it lets every bloc block the reforms.
